planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in full sun to bright light in fast-draining cactus mix; ornate star cactus needs excellent drainage and grows slowly, taking years to reach flowering size.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in full sun to bright light in fast-draining cactus mix; ornate star cactus needs excellent drainage and grows slowly, taking years to reach flowering size. A tall, ribbed, columnar cactus is patterned with scattered flecks of white, star-like wool against dark green skin, arranged along pronounced vertical ribs edged with stiff yellow-brown spines, eventually producing large, pale yellow flowers at the crown once the plant matures after many years. Native to central Mexico, it is prized by collectors for its striking geometric ribbing and starry white speckling, growing slowly into an impressive columnar specimen over a decade or more of patient cultivation. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide as much direct sun as possible for tight, well-defined ribs, and protect from frost and excess winter moisture.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in full sun to bright light in fast-draining cactus mix; Goat's Horn Cactus needs excellent drainage and is slow-growing, taking several years to reach flowering size.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in full sun to bright light in fast-draining cactus mix; Goat's Horn Cactus needs excellent drainage and is slow-growing, taking several years to reach flowering size. A rounded, ribbed, blue-gray body speckled with fine white wool is armed with dramatically long, curved, twisting dark spines that curl outward like a goat's horns, one of the most distinctively spined of all the star cactus species and a favorite of collectors for that ornamental spination alone. Native to the Chihuahuan Desert of northern Mexico, it produces large, funnel-shaped yellow flowers with a reddish throat once mature, but is grown by most collectors chiefly for its dramatic curling spines and silvery-blue, woolly-speckled body. Water only when the soil is fully dry, provide strong direct sun for the best spine development and body color, and protect from frost and winter wet.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining cactus mix; brain cactus needs excellent drainage and its thin, wavy ribs are prone to sunburn if moved into intense sun too quickly.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in bright light to full sun in fast-draining cactus mix; brain cactus needs excellent drainage and its thin, wavy ribs are prone to sunburn if moved into intense sun too quickly. Numerous thin, tightly packed, undulating ribs wind around a rounded body in a convoluted, folded pattern that closely resembles a brain, an unusual and instantly recognizable form among globe cacti, topped with delicate, pale pink to lavender flowers with a darker central stripe in spring. Native to central Mexico, it is a popular novelty cactus for its bizarre, sculptural rib pattern, and its relatively small size makes it well suited to a windowsill collection or mixed cactus dish garden. Water only when the soil is fully dry, acclimate gradually to strong direct sun to avoid scorching the thin ribs, and protect from frost.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in full sun in fast-draining cactus mix; Turk's Cap Cactus needs consistent warmth year-round and excellent drainage, and does not tolerate any frost.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in full sun in fast-draining cactus mix; Turk's Cap Cactus needs consistent warmth year-round and excellent drainage, and does not tolerate any frost. A ribbed, barrel-shaped green body armed with stout amber spines grows for years before eventually producing a distinctive woolly, bristled, cap-like structure called a cephalium at its crown, from which small pink flowers and bright red-pink fruit emerge in succession for the rest of the plant's life, resembling a fez or turban perched atop the cactus. Native to the Caribbean islands, it requires many years of growth before the cephalium forms, after which the main body stops growing wider and channels its energy into flowering and fruiting from the cap. Water sparingly and only in warm weather, provide full sun, and keep it consistently warm, since it is more cold-sensitive than most desert cacti and can be damaged by even brief chilly, damp conditions.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in full sun to bright light in extremely fast-draining, mineral cactus mix; Copiapoa is adapted to one of the driest deserts on Earth and needs minimal water and impeccable drainage.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or xeriscape container in full sun to bright light in extremely fast-draining, mineral cactus mix; Copiapoa is adapted to one of the driest deserts on Earth and needs minimal water and impeccable drainage. A rounded, slow-growing body is coated in a chalky, ashy-gray to bluish-white bloom that gives the whole plant a striking pale, ghostly appearance, with a dense cluster of dark spines and black woolly hair at the crown, eventually offsetting into a mounded, sculptural cluster over many years. Native to the fog-fed coastal Atacama Desert of Chile, among the driest places on Earth, it survives largely on the moisture in coastal fog rather than rainfall, making it extremely intolerant of overwatering in cultivation. Water very sparingly and only during the warmest months, provide maximum direct sun, and use a gritty, fast-draining, largely mineral potting mix to replicate its harsh native conditions.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference

planting.note: Grow as a houseplant or shaded hanging basket in bright, indirect light in a loose, well-drained, chunky epiphytic mix; rat tail cactus is an epiphytic forest cactus and prefers more humidity and less intense sun than desert cacti.

directions: Grow as a houseplant or shaded hanging basket in bright, indirect light in a loose, well-drained, chunky epiphytic mix; rat tail cactus is an epiphytic forest cactus and prefers more humidity and less intense sun than desert cacti. Long, thin, trailing, spine-covered stems cascade densely from a hanging basket, growing several feet long over time, and in spring the plant produces a profusion of brilliant magenta-pink, tubular flowers all along the trailing stems, a spectacular flush of color from an otherwise unassuming, snake-like plant. Native to Mexican and Central American forests, where it grows draped over tree branches rather than rooted in desert soil, it appreciates more regular watering and higher humidity than typical desert cacti, though it still stores water in its fleshy stems and should not sit in soggy mix. Hang where its long trailing stems can cascade freely, water when the mix approaches dryness, and avoid disturbing the plant while flower buds are forming, since they can drop if the pot is moved or turned.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America reference
